stem: The graph of the exponential function $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x}+q$, with $b>0$, has the horizontal asymptote $y={=q}$. The graph cuts the $y$-axis at the point $A(0, {=p})$ and passes through the point $B({=n}, {=r})$. Determine the equation of $f$, in the form $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x}+q$.
solution: The horizontal asymptote of $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x}+q$ is the line $y=q$. The asymptote is $y={=q}$, so $q={=q}$ and $f(x)=a\cdot b^{x} {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Substitute the $y$-intercept $A(0, {=p})$. Since $b^{0}=1$, we get ${=p}=a\cdot b^{0} {=qop} {=qabs}$, so ${=p}=a {=qop} {=qabs}$.
Isolate the power of $b$: ${=r} {=qneg} {=qabs}={=a}\cdot b^{{=n}}$, so ${=d}={=a}\cdot b^{{=n}}$. Divide by ${=a}$: $b^{{=n}}=\frac{{=d}}{{=a}}={=pw}$.
notes:
Text-only restatement of the book's ex6-5-7a figure (asymptote, y-intercept A, second point B). The book's figure shows the asymptote as a dashed line, so the stem states it; b>0 is stated so b is unique. Twist beyond ex6-5-7a: the asymptote is not the x-axis (q is never 0) and a is not 1, so the student reads q from the asymptote, finds a from the y-intercept, and only then finds b from the second point (three unknowns). Method is exactly the book's: q from the asymptote, then substitute points. Parameters: b in {2,3}, second point at x=2 or 3, a in +-1..3, q in -5..5 excluding 0, |a*b^n| <= 30, giving 200 distinct instances. Because a and b^n are both positive when b>0, the sign of a decides whether the curve lies above or below its asymptote (sign-of-a-lost is the typical wrong answer when the point A lies below the asymptote). The sign of q is rendered through let-params qop/qneg holding '+' or '-' (string literals); if the engine refuses string literals in let, replace them with signed(q).

The app's marker reads f(x) (or g(x)) on one side of an equation as y (answer-marker.ts fnName), so the key names the dependent variable the way the pipeline's parser can: 'y = {=a}*{=b}^x {=qop} {=qabs}', with the variables ['x', 'y'] (as the sibling identify-function writes 'y = m*x + c'). A student's 'f(x) = ...' or 'y = ...' is marked the same. The stem (which still asks for the form f(x)=... / g(x)=...), the answer's value and the worked solution are unchanged.
